builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: SysPilot: Cross-Library Performance Autotuning via Library Performance Contracts
summary: The method replaces application-specific manual tuning and general-purpose autotuners with reusable Library Performance Contracts that encode resource demands and observability signals across libraries. It requires contract synthesis from documentation and code artifacts plus profiling runs to validate conflict hypotheses, which adds specification and instrumentation complexity. It can fail when contracts are incomplete or inaccurate, when contention patterns shift across deployments, or when the target libraries lack sufficient observability to validate the derived hypotheses.
rationale: The technique targets CPU-bound cross-library resource contention rather than GPU or LLM-serving bottlenecks typical of this reader's infrastructure, and its benefits depend on contract quality and workload profiling that are not yet validated at small production scale.
technique: Cross-library autotuning via Library Performance Contracts

claims.statement: The method replaces application-specific manual tuning and general-purpose autotuners with reusable Library Performance Contracts that encode resource demands and observability signals across libraries. It requires contract synthesis from documentation and code artifacts plus profiling runs to validate conflict hypotheses, which adds specification and instrumentation complexity. It can fail when contracts are incomplete or inaccurate, when contention patterns shift across deployments, or when the target libraries lack sufficient observability to validate the derived hypotheses.
Improves benchmark performance metrics by up to 38% over the best configuration found by general-purpose autotuners such as OpenTuner and SMAC3, while using 3x fewer runs.
